opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one of the things that really struck me when we were working on InstructGPT was how well the instruction-following behavior generalized to settings we basically never trained on. Almost all of our fine-tuning data was in English, and our labelers were mostly writing English prompts. Yet the model would follow instructions in French, German, Japanese, and other languages much better than the base model did. Similarly, very little of our data was about code, but the model got noticeably better at following instructions about code too.

That's puzzling in a good way, but it's also puzzling in a way I don't fully understand. Why does it work? One story is that the pretrained model already has a fairly general concept of "do what the person is asking for," and fine-tuning mostly selects or amplifies that concept rather than teaching something new. If that's right, a relatively small amount of human feedback can steer a lot of behavior. That would be really encouraging for alignment.

But the flip side is that we don't have a good theory for *which* things generalize and which don't. Sometimes the model picks up the spirit of what you wanted. Sometimes it picks up some surface feature of the training data, like a certain tone or format, and generalizes that instead. We mostly find out empirically, after the fact.

And that matters a lot for the long-term picture. Eventually we want to train models on tasks where humans can evaluate the answers, and have them behave well on tasks where we *can't* easily evaluate them, because they're too hard or too complex. Whether that works is fundamentally a generalization question. Does the model learn "tell the truth," or does it learn "say what the evaluator will think is true"? On the easy tasks those look identical, and only diverge on the hard ones. So I think understanding generalization better, and being able to measure it, is one of the most important open problems. It's one reason I'm excited about experiments where you deliberately train on easy cases and test on hard ones, so you can study this directly instead of just hoping it works out.

r001.rationale: The response says InstructGPT’s fine-tuning data was almost entirely in English, yet it followed instructions in French, German, Japanese, and other languages better than the base model.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that still surprises me is how much you get for free. When we were doing the early InstructGPT work, we fine-tuned on a pretty narrow slice of human demonstrations and preference comparisons. The datasets were mostly English, mostly a particular kind of task, written by a relatively small group of contractors. And then you'd go test the model and it would follow instructions in French or in Python, or it would respond sensibly to a type of request nobody had ever written a demonstration for. We weren't training "be helpful in French." We were training on a few tens of thousands of examples, and somehow the model picked up something more abstract like "the human wants a thing, go do the thing."

And the puzzling part isn't that it generalizes. Pretraining gives you this enormous latent competence, so maybe you should expect it. The puzzling part is that we don't really have a good account of which direction it generalizes in. You push on the model in one place, and it moves in a bunch of other places, and you only find out which ones by poking at it afterward. Sometimes that's great. Sometimes you teach it to be cautious about one category of harm and it becomes weirdly preachy about cooking recipes.

So the question I keep coming back to is: what is the model actually learning when we do this? Is it learning our intentions, or is it learning a stylistic shorthand that happens to correlate with our intentions on the distribution we tested? Those two things look identical in the training data and very different once you leave it. And for alignment, that distinction is the whole game. If the generalization is tracking the right thing, we're in reasonably good shape as we scale. If it's tracking a proxy, then the better the model gets, the better it gets at the proxy, and we might not notice until it matters a lot.

What makes it hard to study is that you can't just read it off the weights, and you can't enumerate all the situations you care about. So you end up with this empirical science of generalization where you deliberately train on one distribution and test far away from it, and try to figure out the rules. We've started to get some results there, things like training on easy problems and seeing how well it transfers to hard ones, but honestly I'd say we understand it about as well as people understood scaling laws before anyone wrote them down. There's clearly structure. We just haven't found the clean description yet.

astra-6.text:
One thing I find puzzling is how much the models seem to generalize from relatively little instruction training. You train them on a particular set of requests, and then you can ask them to do something quite different, and they’ll often make a reasonable attempt. Somehow they’ve learned something broader than just how to answer the questions you trained them on.

But what exactly is that broader thing? Is it “follow the user’s instructions”? Is it “produce the sort of answer a human evaluator would like”? In the training setting, those might lead to very similar behavior. In a new situation, they could lead to quite different behavior.

So the puzzling part is that generalization works remarkably well, but we don’t have a very good handle on what determines its direction. And for alignment, that’s a central question: when the model encounters a situation we didn’t train it on, which of the many possible lessons from training will it apply?

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I find puzzling is how much instruction training seems to generalize from a relatively narrow set of examples. You train a model to follow certain kinds of instructions, and then it can follow instructions in situations that look quite different from anything you explicitly trained it on.

But that leaves a really important question: what has it actually learned? Has it learned something like, “Understand what the user wants and help them achieve it”? Or has it learned a collection of patterns that happen to produce helpful-looking answers in the situations we test?

Those explanations can look very similar on familiar tasks and come apart in new circumstances. So the puzzle isn’t just why generalization works so well. It’s how to tell which part of the behavior will generalize, and whether it’s the part we actually wanted.
